def: When a stone keeps some colours of the light that goes through it. What is missing in the spectrum is the trace of what colours the stone.
One of the five qualities of a gem: the market must want it and trust it (no hidden treatment, no synthetic sold as natural), and the law must allow it to be sold.
A material made of small crystals pointing in all directions (jade, chalcedony, lapis lazuli). Between crossed polarizing filters, it stays bright.
Without a regular order at the scale of the atoms: opal, obsidian, glass.
The angle beyond which all the light coming from the glass towards the stone is sent back into the glass. It makes the shadow edge of the refractometer.
Said of a stone that splits light into two rays (uniaxial or biaxial). In the polariscope, it lights up and goes dark four times per turn.
A four- or six-rayed star seen on a cabochon, caused by fine aligned needles (star rubies and star sapphires).
A direction in a crystal along which light is not split into two rays. A uniaxial stone has one, a biaxial stone has two.
A balance that weighs a stone in air and then in water, to work out the density with Archimedes' principle.
A stone with two optic axes and three refractive indices (orthorhombic, monoclinic and triclinic systems).
The difference between the largest and the smallest index of an anisotropic stone. It is measured with the refractometer.
A stone cut as a smooth, domed surface, without facets. The hardness test can be done under its base.
The unit of weight of stones: 1 carat = 0.2 gram (so 1 g = 5 ct). The word comes from the carob seed.
The way a stone breaks when there is no plane of weakness. Conchoidal (in arcs, like a shell) or splintery (fibrous).
A soft leather cloth used to wipe the stone before looking at it, to remove dust and grease.
A small coloured filter that only lets through yellow-green and deep red. Chromium (and cobalt) turns red under the filter, iron does not.
The degree of purity of a stone: the more visible inclusions, the lower the clarity.
The splitting of a stone along a smooth plane, where the bonds between atoms are weaker. Diamond, topaz, fluorite and kunzite have it.
A polariscope fitted with a lens, which shows the interference figure of a stone and so tells uniaxial from biaxial.
How easily a material carries heat away. Diamond is the best known conductor.
A synthetic diamond obtained by growing diamond layer by layer from a gas. It is a real diamond.
The ratio between the weight of a stone and that of the same volume of water. Each species has its own (quartz 2.65, diamond 3.52, corundum 4.0).
A small instrument that separates the two directions of vibration of light and shows side by side the colours of a pleochroic stone.
A treatment that makes an element (titanium, chromium, beryllium) enter the surface of a stone to colour it. The layer is sometimes no thicker than 0.1 mm.
The difference in refractive index between blue light and red light. It gives a stone its “fire” (very strong in diamond, sphene and demantoid).
The quality of a gem that lasts: it resists scratches (hardness), blows (toughness) and its environment (stability).
The resistance of a stone to scratching. It is placed on the Mohs scale (from 1 to 10).
The way the surface of a stone reflects light: vitreous, adamantine, resinous, greasy, silky, metallic, pearly…
X-ray fluorescence spectrometry: X-rays make every chemical element of the stone answer with its own lines. Fast, and it leaves no trace.
Chemical elements present in tiny amounts (iron, chromium, vanadium, titanium, gallium…). Their proportions vary from one deposit to another.
A small flat surface polished on a cut stone.
The visible glow of a stone that absorbs ultraviolet light and gives it back as visible light. It stops when the lamp is switched off.
Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy: it detects chemical bonds, so oil, resin or water in a stone.
The pattern seen in the conoscope: a black cross and coloured rings (uniaxial) or two eyes and a moustache (biaxial).
A material, most often a mineral, with enough beauty, rarity, durability, value and acceptability to be worn as jewellery or collected.
The outer shape of a crystal (needle, prism, plate), linked to the speed of growth along each axis.
High pressure, high temperature: a process that makes synthetic diamonds, or that lightens or removes the colour of some natural diamonds.
A material that looks like a gem without being one (coloured glass, cubic zirconia sold as a diamond).
A foreign body, cavity or crack trapped in a stone. Inclusions tell how it formed and help tell natural from synthetic.
A number that says how much light is slowed down and bent in a stone. It is measured with the refractometer.
Said of a stone that does not split light (cubic or amorphous: garnet, spinel, glass). It has a single refractive index.
Laser ablation mass spectrometry: a laser vaporizes a microscopic amount of matter, which is analysed to measure the trace elements. The reference method for origin.
The border between the bright zone and the dark zone in the refractometer. Its position on the scale gives the index.
Light given off by a stone: fluorescence (which stops with the lamp) or phosphorescence (which goes on).
Two crystals of the same nature joined, one being the mirror image of the other.
Synthetic silicon carbide that looks like diamond. It conducts heat like diamond, but it also conducts electricity.
A gem formed without human help, even if people later cut or treated it.
The deposit a stone comes from. It strongly changes the value of a ruby, a sapphire or an emerald and is worked out from the trace elements.
A glow that goes on for a few seconds after the UV lamp is switched off.
The property of a coloured stone to show different colours depending on the direction of observation: two (dichroism, uniaxial) or three (trichroism, biaxial).
Two crossed polarizing filters between which the stone is turned. It tells isotropic, anisotropic and aggregate apart.
A laser spectroscopy that gives the signature of the crystal lattice of a mineral: it identifies it with certainty, even for a tiny inclusion.
One of the five qualities of a gem: the rarer a good stone is, the more it is sought after.
Beyond the critical angle, all the light is sent back into the glass of the refractometer.
An instrument that measures the refractive index of a stone with the critical angle, using a drop of contact liquid.
The change of direction of light when it goes from one medium to another (Descartes' law).
Fine parallel needles in a natural ruby or sapphire, which scatter light like silk.
The spectrum of light after it has gone through a stone: the dark lines and bands are what the stone absorbed. It is the fingerprint of its colour.
A small prism (or grating) that spreads out the light that went through the stone, to read its absorption lines.
The resistance of a stone to light, heat, chemicals and humidity.
A gem made by people with the same composition and structure as a natural gem (a synthetic ruby is a real corundum).
The way atoms are arranged: there are seven systems (cubic, tetragonal, hexagonal, trigonal, orthorhombic, monoclinic, triclinic).
The resistance of a stone to blows. Jade is the toughest gem; diamond, though very hard, is not as tough.
An operation that improves the look of a stone (heating, irradiation, dyeing, filling…). It is allowed as long as it is disclosed.
The ability of a stone to let light through: transparent, translucent or opaque.
A stone with a single optic axis and two refractive indices (tetragonal, hexagonal and trigonal systems).
An invisible radiation beyond violet. The cabinet has two lamps: long-wave UV (365 nm) and short-wave UV (254 nm).
